headline: Florida Plants 9,000 Milkweed Along Highways to Save Monarchs
meta_description: Florida is transforming roadside margins into vital habitat for monarch butterflies by planting 9,000 milkweed plants across six counties.
summary_short: Researchers in Florida are planting milkweed along roadsides to create a migration corridor for monarchs, with 9,000 plants already in the ground.
body:
Florida's roadsides are becoming an unexpected lifeline for monarch butterflies. Researchers have planted 9,000 milkweed plants along roads in six North Florida counties, with 6,000 more planned before 2029. Monarchs are already appearing at these sites, drawn to the plants they depend on for survival. The initiative is part of a broader national effort led by the University of Illinois Chicago to repurpose managed land—road margins, power line easements, and rail corridors—into functional habitat for monarchs and other pollinators. Florida's Department of Transportation joined the project in 2024, committing to manage 10,200 acres of roadside land for conservation.

The choice of milkweed is deliberate and scientifically sound. Monarch caterpillars have evolved to eat only milkweed, storing the plant's toxic compounds in their tissues to make themselves unpalatable to predators. Without milkweed, monarchs cannot survive. For adult butterflies facing migration routes exceeding 100 miles daily, a continuous corridor of nectar-rich plants provides essential fuel. Jaret Daniels, curator of Lepidoptera at the Florida Museum of Natural History, notes that this approach works with existing infrastructure rather than against it. "Roadsides are managed regardless," he explains, "so why not do so in a way that confers greater benefits?"

The team selected two native species suited to Florida's sandy roadsides: pinewoods milkweed and butterfly weed. Because pinewoods milkweed isn't commercially available, researchers hand-collect seeds from wild populations during flowering season, achieving 98 percent germination rates at the University of Florida Native Plant Nursery. Planting occurs during winter when crews can work without Florida's summer heat, and designated wildflower zones now bloom across multiple sites. The data gathered will guide expansion into other counties and states, transforming how we think about conservation on land we already maintain.
quick_facts: 9,000 milkweed plants planted along Florida roadsides in six counties
Monarch caterpillars can only eat milkweed; no other food source exists
Adult monarchs travel over 100 miles daily during migration
Florida Department of Transportation managing 10,200 acres for pollinator habitat
Pinewoods milkweed seeds achieved 98 percent germination rate
